title: Monolithic Engine or Emergent Network?: General Intelligence (g-Factor), the CHC Hierarchy, and Psychometric Non-Identifiability on Trial — From Spearman's 1904 tetrad differences and attenuation math to Cattell-Horn fluid/crystallized intelligence and Carroll's 1993 Three-Stratum CHC consensus; Deary, Penke & Johnson's parieto-frontal white-matter tract & Lothian longevity synthesis plus Jansen et al.'s 2020 GWAS overlap across 269,867 individuals; van der Maas's 2006 Lotka-Volterra mutualism proof of psychometric non-identifiability, Kovacs & Conway's 2016 formative executive-bottleneck Process Overlap Theory & Spearman's Law of Diminishing Returns, and Ritchie & Tucker-Drob's 2018 causal +1 to +5 IQ/year schooling gains

teenKit.tldr: If someone is great at one mental test, they are usually great at all of them, but scientists are deeply split on whether this means the brain has a single general intelligence engine or is just a network of independent skills helping each other grow.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how our minds work impacts everything from how schools are designed to how we diagnose learning differences and measure human potential.
keyTakeaways: The 'positive manifold' shows that scores across completely different mental tests almost always correlate positively with one another.
Traditional psychometrics view this through hierarchical models like CHC, placing a general 'g-factor' at the top of human cognitive ability.
Rival theories like Dynamic Mutualism and Process Overlap Theory prove that a universal score can emerge naturally from independent skills interacting and strengthening each other over time.

vocab.meaning: The stubborn statistical rule where people who score high on one cognitive test tend to score high on all other cognitive tests, no matter how different they are.
A theoretical single core engine of general intelligence proposed to drive overall performance across all mental tasks.
The theory that a general intelligence score is an illusion created by different brain modules boosting each other's growth during childhood development.
The idea that general intelligence is actually the result of a few shared executive 'bottlenecks' in the brain, like working memory, that are required for many different tasks.

quiz.question: What is the 'positive manifold' in intelligence testing?
options: The fact that test scores improve every single year globally
The tendency for people who do well on one mental test to do well on others
The psychological boost students get from receiving praise
The correlation between high physical health and high brain volume
quiz.explanation: The positive manifold describes how almost all cognitive test scores correlate positively with each other rather than being random or negative.

quiz.question: How does Dynamic Mutualism explain the existence of the g-factor?
options: As a single genetic gene passed down from parents
As a physical CPU-like engine sitting in the frontal lobe
As an illusion generated when independent mental skills boost each other's development over time
As a statistical error caused by poorly calibrated testing clocks
quiz.explanation: Dynamic mutualism proves that completely independent cognitive modules interacting during childhood can mathematically produce a single unified g-factor.

quiz.question: What did Ritchie and Tucker-Drob discover about the effect of compulsory schooling on IQ?
options: Schooling has zero measurable impact on intelligence test scores
Extra years of education reliably and causally lift IQ points through specific skill gains
Schooling only improves vocabulary while harming spatial reasoning
Only private schooling produces any shift in psychometric scores
quiz.explanation: Their massive meta-analysis showed that each extra year of compulsory education causes a direct gain of one to five IQ points.
